analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million at 2% and above $1 billion at 3% to 6%.
analysis.headline: The wealth tax bill drew 37 Democratic cosponsors but never got a committee vote, dying in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new annual federal tax on net wealth — everything a person owns minus debts — charged only on fortunes above $50 million: 2% on wealth from $50 million to $1 billion, and 3% on wealth above that, rising to 6% if Congress ever passes a universal health insurance program that replaces duplicate private coverage. It directs the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers each year, funds more IRS enforcement and taxpayer service, and adds rules to catch assets parked in offshore accounts and family trusts. Households worth under $50 million would pay nothing under it.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with net worth below $50 million — nearly everyone — pay nothing directly, while the tax falls only on the very wealthiest; the bill also funds more IRS taxpayer services and enforcement, and the top rate is designed to double if a universal health care program covering everyone is enacted.

how_it_helps.text: The tax starts only above $50 million in net wealth: 2% on the portion up to $1 billion and 3% above that, with married couples treated as one taxpayer, so no household under $50 million owes anything.

The rate on billion-dollar fortunes doubles to 6% in any year in which legislation is in effect providing comprehensive universal health coverage that bars duplicate private insurance, tying the wealthiest tax rate to universal coverage.

The bill directs the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers each year and authorizes $70 billion for tax enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business systems modernization through fiscal 2034.

It adds anti-avoidance measures: rules to unmask assets shifted into foreign corporations, partnerships, and trusts, an exit tax of 40% on covered expatriates, and attribution rules treating property moved to young family members as still belonging to the giver.

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $50 million in net worth, including hard-to-value holdings like private businesses, art, and boats, which count toward the tax; payers facing liquidity constraints can defer payment up to five years.

drawbacks.text: Valuing fortunes is hard: the bill acknowledges that many assets have no readily ascertainable value and authorizes the Treasury to use new formulaic and retrospective valuation methods, which would invite disputes, penalties (up to 50% for gross valuation misstatements), and years of litigation.

Enforcing it is expensive by design: the bill authorizes $100 billion in appropriations over a decade and requires annual audits of at least 30% of wealth-tax payers, so the net revenue depends on how well that machinery works.

Wealthy households could push back through the deferral option — up to five years for liquidity constraints or hardship to an ongoing enterprise — and the 40% exit tax acknowledges the risk of the very rich giving up citizenship to escape the tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is aimed squarely at the top sliver of wealth holders and costs everyone below $50 million nothing, which is a straightforward shift of tax burden upward; the serious cost is administrative, since pricing private companies, art, and trusts every year is genuinely difficult and the bill bets heavily on new IRS valuation methods, expanded funding, and aggressive auditing to make it stick.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced March 20, 2024 and sent straight to the House Ways and Means Committee, the bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on March 20, 2024, with dozens of original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
In total 37 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households that would have owed the tax — those with more than $50 million in net wealth — are better off, since a bill that never received a committee vote cannot become law; supporters of the tax gained nothing beyond a public record of 37 Democratic signatures.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats — about 17% of the House Democratic caucus — and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, so the bill died entirely within a Democratic minority faction while the Republican-held committee declined to act.

industries.note: The bill would put a new 2%-to-6% annual levy directly on their fortunes, including homes, art, boats, private businesses, and trust holdings. Their interest in this bill runs against the public's: the tax's cost falls only on them, and its relief falls on everyone else through a lighter tax burden on ordinary earners.

industries.industry: Private wealth, trust, and offshore asset management
industries.note: The bill targets the structures this industry sells — grantor trusts, trusts benefiting minors, split-interest trusts, and foreign holding entities — with attribution rules, reporting mandates, and new valuation powers, shrinking its tax-avoidance business; at the same time, compliance and valuation work would generate fees. Its core service of shielding large fortunes from tax is what the bill exists to close.
